children.name: Balearica
children.description: Crowned cranes — the most ancient crane lineage, distinguished by their stiff golden crest of wiry feathers atop the head and their ability to perch in trees, a behaviour unique among cranes. They inhabit African savanna wetlands and grasslands. The display of a crowned crane — bowing, leaping, and calling with its inflatable red throat pouch — is one of the most elaborate in the bird world.

children.name: Balearica pavonina
children.description: The black crowned crane (Balearica pavonina) is a part of the family Gruidae, along with its sister species, the grey crowned crane.

children.name: Balearica regulorum
children.description: The grey crowned crane or gray crowned crane (Balearica regulorum) is a large crane species native to Sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Leucogeranus
children.description: The Siberian crane — a critically endangered, pure white crane that breeds in the Arctic tundra of eastern Siberia and winters in a single wetland in China (Poyang Lake). Its haunting, flute-like calls and spectacular migration route made it a cultural icon in Russia and China. The entire eastern population funnels through Poyang Lake, making it extremely vulnerable to habitat change. A separate central population migrating to India has been functionally extinct since 2002.

children.name: Leucogeranus leucogeranus
children.description: The Siberian crane (Leucogeranus leucogeranus), also known as the Siberian white crane or the snow crane, is a bird of the family Gruidae, the cranes.

children.name: Grus
children.description: The true cranes — tall, long-legged birds of open wetlands and grasslands whose bugling calls and spectacular migration concentrations make them among the most iconic of all Palearctic birds. The common crane (trana) is Sweden's defining migratory spectacle: each April, over 100,000 cranes converge on Lake Hornborga in Västergötland to rest and refuel before continuing north to their breeding grounds, making it one of the greatest wildlife events in Europe. Cranes are among the longest-lived birds, forming pair bonds that last decades and engaging in elaborate dancing displays — leaping, wing-spreading, and bowing — that strengthen their partnership. In Sweden, the crane's resonant, bugling 'trrop trrop' call is so deeply embedded in the national consciousness that it has become synonymous with the arrival of spring.

children.name: Grus grus
children.description: The common crane, also known as the Eurasian crane, is a bird of the family Gruidae, the cranes. A medium-sized species, it is the only crane commonly found in Europe besides the demoiselle crane and the Siberian crane that only are regular in the far eastern part of the continent. Along with the sandhill crane, demoiselle crane and the brolga, it is one of only four crane species not currently classified as threatened with extinction or conservation dependent on the species level.

children.name: Grus japonensis
children.description: The red-crowned crane, also called the Japanese crane and the Manchurian crane, is a large Northeast Asian crane among the rarest cranes in the world. In some parts of its range, it is known as a symbol of luck, longevity, and fidelity.

children.name: Grus antigone
children.description: The sarus crane (Antigone antigone) is a large nonmigratory crane found in parts of the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, and northern Australia.

children.name: Grus canadensis
children.description: The sandhill crane (Antigone canadensis) is a species of large crane of North America and extreme northeastern Siberia.

children.name: Grus monacha
children.description: The hooded crane (Grus monacha) is a crane native to East Asia and a frequent migratory bird in Japan.

children.name: Grus americana
children.description: The whooping crane (Grus americana) is an endangered crane species, native to North America, with an estimated 22–30+ year life expectancy in the wild.

children.name: Anthropoides
children.description: Demoiselle cranes and blue cranes — elegant, relatively small cranes of dry steppes and semi-arid grasslands far removed from the wetland habitats favoured by most of their relatives. The demoiselle crane is the world's smallest crane, breeding across the central Asian steppes from the Black Sea to Mongolia and wintering in India. Its name comes from French — given by Marie Antoinette who was charmed by its dainty, graceful appearance — and it is indeed a bird of extraordinary elegance: grey-bodied with a long white ear-tuft, a black neck and breast, and long decorative tertial feathers that droop over the tail. Demoiselle cranes are rare but annual vagrants to Scandinavia, typically appearing in spring among flocks of common cranes at staging sites such as Lake Hornborga.

children.name: Anthropoides virgo

children.name: Bugeranus

It is restricted to the undisturbed wetlands and floodplains of Central and Southern Africa and is the most habitat-specialist of all crane species, requiring large, pristine marshes with deep water. Its bugling call is deeper and more resonant than that of any other African crane.

children.name: Rallus madagascariensis
children.description: The Madagascar rail (Rallus madagascariensis) is a species of bird in the family Rallidae.

children.name: Rallus tenuirostris
children.description: The Aztec rail or Mexican rail, (Rallus tenuirostris) is a Near Threatened species of bird in subfamily Rallinae of family Rallidae, the rails, gallinules, and coots.

children.name: Rougetius
children.description: Rougetius — a genus of rails & coots in the family Rallidae.

children.name: Sarothrura
children.description: Sarothrura — a genus of rails & coots in the family Rallidae.

children.name: Sarothrura affinis
children.description: The striped flufftail (Sarothrura affinis) is a species of bird in the flufftail family Sarothruridae.

children.name: Sarothrura insularis
children.description: The Madagascar flufftail (Sarothrura insularis) is a species of bird in the family Sarothruridae.

children.name: Vitirallus
children.description: Vitirallus - a genus in the family Rallidae.

children.name: Wanshuina
children.description: Wanshuina — a genus of rails & coots in the family Rallidae.

children.name: Zapornia
children.description: Zapornia - a genus in the family Rallidae.

children.name: Otis
children.description: The great bustard — a monotypic genus containing the heaviest flying bird on Earth. Male Great Bustards can weigh up to 21 kg, yet they fly powerfully with deep, slow wingbeats. Once widespread across European grasslands, they have declined dramatically due to agricultural intensification.

children.name: Otis tarda
children.description: The great bustard (Otis tarda) is a bird in the bustard family, and the only living member of the genus Otis.

children.name: Chlamydotis
children.description: The houbara bustards — medium-sized bustards of arid regions, known for their spectacular courtship displays in which males raise a white ruff of neck feathers and run in circles. They are highly prized by falconers in the Middle East, leading to intensive conservation breeding programmes.

children.name: Chlamydotis undulata
children.description: The African houbara (Chlamydotis undulata), also known as the houbara bustard (houbara from for bustards in general), is a relatively small bustard native to North Africa, where it lives in arid habitats.

children.name: Chlamydotis macqueenii
children.description: The Asian houbara (Chlamydotis macqueenii), also known as MacQueen's bustard, is a large bird in the bustard family.

children.name: Tetrax
children.description: The little bustard — a monotypic genus of small, compact bustards found across southern Europe, North Africa, and Asia. Unlike their larger relatives, little bustards are gregarious, forming large flocks in winter. They are fast runners and explosive fliers.

children.name: Tetrax tetrax
children.description: The little bustard (Tetrax tetrax) is a bird in the bustard family, the only member of the genus Tetrax.

children.name: Ardeotis
children.description: The largest bustards, found in Africa, Asia, and Australia. They are among the heaviest flying birds.

children.name: Ardeotis kori
children.description: The kori bustard (Ardeotis kori) is the largest flying bird native to Africa.

children.name: Ardeotis arabs
children.description: The Arabian bustard (Ardeotis arabs) is a species of bustard which is found across the Sahel region of Africa and south western Arabia.

children.name: Ardeotis australis
children.description: The Australian bustard (Ardeotis australis) is a large ground-dwelling bird that is common in grassland, woodland and open agricultural country across northern Australia and southern New Guinea.

children.name: Neotis
children.description: Medium to large bustards found in sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Neotis cafra
children.description: A bustard found in southern Africa.

children.name: Eupodotis
children.description: Small to medium bustards found in Africa.

children.name: Eupodotis caerulescens
children.description: The blue korhaan or blue bustard (Eupodotis caerulescens) is a species of bird in the family Otididae which is native to South Africa.

children.name: Eupodotis vigorsii
children.description: The karoo korhaan (Heterotetrax vigorsii), also known as karoo bustard, is a species of bird in the bustard family, Otididae, from Southern Africa.

children.name: Lophotis
children.description: Small bustards with distinctive crests, found in Africa.

children.name: Afrotis
children.description: Small black bustards from southern Africa.

children.name: Lophotis
children.description: Bustards with distinctive crests from Africa.

children.name: Heliornis
children.description: A monotypic genus of the smallest and most colourful finfoot, distinguished by strikingly patterned feet and a slender, pointed bill. It is the only New World representative of the family.

children.name: Podica
children.description: A large, robust finfoot with a long graduated tail and a distinctive white throat patch. It inhabits forested rivers and streams across sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Podica senegalensis
children.description: The African finfoot or Peter's finfoot (Podica senegalensis) is an aquatic bird from the family Heliornithidae (the finfoots and sungrebe).

children.name: Heliopais
children.description: A monotypic Asian genus of finfoot with a distinctive black mask and a thick neck. It is one of the most threatened waterbirds in Southeast Asia due to habitat loss.

children.name: Heliopais personatus
children.description: The masked finfoot or Asian finfoot (Heliopais personatus) is a highly endangered aquatic bird that was formerly distributed throughout the fresh and brackish wetlands of the eastern Indian subcontinent, Indochina, Malaysia and Indonesia.

children.name: Sarothrura
children.description: Small, secretive rails with a distinctive fluffy tail that is often cocked upright. Males and females often show striking sexual dimorphism, with males more colourful and females more cryptic. They are found across sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar.

children.name: Sarothrura affinis
children.description: The striped flufftail (Sarothrura affinis) is a species of bird in the flufftail family Sarothruridae.

children.name: Sarothrura novae
children.description: This newly discovered species is a small, plump bird with soft downy feathers. It feeds on insects and fruits in dense forest understory.

children.name: Mentocrex hirsuteus
children.description: This species has a distinctive downy appearance, with feathers often tipped in long, curly hairs. It feeds on nectar and small insects.

children.name: Sarothrura pallidula
children.description: The Pale Flufftail has a striking pale plumage, almost white, with subtle barring on the underparts. It feeds primarily on aquatic insects and small crustaceans.

children.name: Mentocrex leucophrys
children.description: Distinctively marked with white plumage and contrasting dark streaks, this species forages in the canopy of tall trees. It feeds on fruit and nectar.

children.name: Mentocrex
children.description: A small genus of forest-dwelling rails endemic to Madagascar, placed in the flufftail family based on genetic evidence. Unlike most flufftails, they lack the distinctive fluffy tail and are more terrestrial in habit.

children.name: Psophia
children.description: Medium-sized, long-legged terrestrial birds with a distinctive humped back, soft plumage and a low, booming call from which their common name derives. They are restricted to the Amazon basin and are important seed dispersers in the rainforest ecosystem.

children.name: Aramus
children.description: A monotypic genus of a long-legged, brown-streaked wading bird with a long, slightly curved bill adapted for extracting snails from their shells. The sole member of its family, it shows features intermediate between rails and cranes.
